When you preface something, you say or write a few words of introduction before getting to your main point. Those introductory words are meant to prepare the listener or reader for what is coming next.

Think of it like clearing the stage before the main performance begins.
To preface = to say or write something preliminary (an opener, a warning, a context-setter) before delivering your actual main message.
The Most Natural Way It Appears

The verb almost always follows one of these two patterns:

Pattern 1: "Preface something with something."

She prefaced her criticism with a compliment.

Pattern 2: "Preface something by saying / by doing."

He prefaced his request by saying he knew it was a big ask.

And one of the most common phrases you will hear in real life is:

"Let me preface this by saying…"

When someone says this, they are signalling: "Before I get to my actual point, I want to say something first to set it up properly."

Example 1:

The doctor prefaced the bad news with a reminder that modern medicine had come a long way.

What's happening: The doctor didn't just blurt out the bad news. First, she said something to mentally prepare the patient. That comforting remark was the preface. The bad news was the main message.

Example 2:

He prefaced his question by admitting he might be wrong.

What's happening: Before asking his question, he put in a humble disclaimer — "I might be wrong about this, but..." — to soften the tone. That disclaimer was the preface.

Example 3:

The professor prefaced her lecture with a five-minute overview of last week's topic.

What's happening: She didn't jump into new material right away. She warmed up the class with a quick recap first. That recap was the preface to the lecture.
What Makes It Different From Simply "Starting" or "Beginning"

This is a subtle but important point.

When you start or begin something, you are simply talking about the first moment of an action. There is no special purpose implied.

When you preface something, there is always a deliberate reason for saying that opening part first. The person is being intentional. The introductory remark serves a purpose — it might be to:

  • Give context so the main point makes sense
  • Soften a blow (like bad news or harsh feedback)
  • Set expectations ("this is going to be a long one")
  • Issue a disclaimer ("I'm not an expert, but…")
  • Show respect or humility before making a bold claim

So preface always carries a sense of purpose and preparation. The opening words are there for a reason, not just happening to come first.

Very often in everyday speech, when someone says "Let me preface this…", the introductory remark is there to protect the main message in some way — to stop it from being misunderstood, to soften it, or to acknowledge its sensitivity. For example:

"Let me preface this by saying I have enormous respect for your work — but I think there are some serious problems with this plan."

Here, the speaker uses the preface as a cushion before delivering a difficult message. This is one of the most common uses in real conversation.

If you can answer yes to all three questions below, the word "preface" fits perfectly:

  1. Is someone saying or writing something before their main point? ✅
  2. Is that opening remark intentional — put there on purpose? ✅
  3. Does the opening remark set up, frame, or prepare the listener/reader for what comes next? ✅
To preface = to deliberately say something first, in order to prepare, frame, or soften what you are actually about to say.
